steps.title: Understand the Fundamental Wave Equation
steps.description: Electromagnetic waves propagate at the speed of light c ≈ 3 × 10^8 m/s. Frequency (f) and wavelength (λ) are inversely proportional: f = c / λ or λ = c / f. Lower frequencies have longer wavelengths that penetrate obstacles and travel long distances, while higher frequencies provide wider bandwidths and higher data rates but suffer higher path loss.

vivaQuestions.q: What is the electromagnetic spectrum?
vivaQuestions.a: The electromagnetic spectrum is the continuous range of all frequencies of electromagnetic radiation, extending from low-frequency radio waves to high-frequency gamma rays.

vivaQuestions.q: What is the mathematical relationship between frequency and wavelength?
vivaQuestions.a: They are inversely proportional: c = f × λ, where c is the speed of light in vacuum (~3 × 10^8 m/s), f is frequency in Hertz (Hz), and λ is wavelength in meters (m).

vivaQuestions.q: What is an ISM band?
vivaQuestions.a: ISM stands for Industrial, Scientific, and Medical radio band. These are portions of the radio spectrum reserved internationally for unlicensed use (e.g., 2.4 GHz and 5.8 GHz), commonly used by Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, and microwave ovens.

vivaQuestions.q: Which frequency band is commonly used by Bluetooth?
vivaQuestions.a: Bluetooth operates in the 2.4 GHz ISM band (specifically 2.402 GHz to 2.480 GHz) using Frequency Hopping Spread Spectrum (FHSS).

vivaQuestions.q: Which frequency bands are used by Wi-Fi?
vivaQuestions.a: Wi-Fi commonly operates in the 2.4 GHz band, the 5 GHz band, and more recently the 6 GHz band (Wi-Fi 6E and Wi-Fi 7).

vivaQuestions.q: What is the difference between licensed and unlicensed spectrum?
vivaQuestions.a: Licensed spectrum is exclusively allocated to specific operators via government auctions/permits (e.g., 4G/5G cellular bands) to guarantee zero interference. Unlicensed spectrum (like ISM bands) is open for public use without licensing, provided devices follow strict transmit power and interference regulations.

vivaQuestions.q: What is the key difference between 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz Wi-Fi?
vivaQuestions.a: 2.4 GHz provides greater physical range and better wall penetration due to longer wavelength, but has only 3 non-overlapping channels and lower speeds. 5 GHz provides much higher data rates and less congestion with 20+ non-overlapping channels, but has shorter coverage range and higher attenuation through obstacles.

conclusion: The experiment demonstrates that wireless communication technologies operate in specific frequency bands selected according to propagation characteristics, bandwidth requirements, interference considerations, and government regulations. Lower frequencies provide greater coverage and obstacle penetration, whereas higher frequencies provide the extensive bandwidth necessary for high-speed multimedia communication.

name: Simulation of Basic Communication System (Tx–Channel–Rx)
problemStatement: Simulate a fundamental end-to-end communication system comprising Transmitter (Tx), Wireless AWGN Channel, and Receiver (Rx) to analyze the impact of additive white Gaussian noise on sinusoidal signal transmission across various standard deviation noise levels.
tasks: Model a signal transmitter producing a sinusoidal carrier waveform.
Model a wireless communication channel corrupted by Additive White Gaussian Noise (AWGN).
Model a signal receiver and visualize the received waveform on a virtual oscilloscope.
Simulate across 5 noise standard deviation levels: σ = 0.0 (clean), 0.1, 0.5, 2.0, and 5.0 (lost).
Record observed waveform behavior and compare transmitted vs. received signal parameters.

variants.label: Python Code
variants.title: End-to-End Tx-Channel-Rx Simulation in Python
variants.description: Python script simulating Transmitter sine wave generation, AWGN wireless channel at 5 noise levels (sigma 0.0 to 5.0), and Receiver multi-panel oscilloscope plotting.
variants.code:
"""
Simulation of Basic Communication System (Tx–Channel–Rx)
Subject: Modern Digital Mobile Communication
Language: Python 3 with NumPy & Matplotlib
"""
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# --- 1. Transmitter Parameters ---
fs = 1000            # Sampling frequency (Hz)
t = np.linspace(0, 1, fs, endpoint=False)  # 1 second duration
freq = 5             # Carrier frequency = 5 Hz
amp = 1.0            # Signal amplitude = 1.0 V
tx_signal = amp * np.sin(2 * np.pi * freq * t)

# --- 2. Channel Impairment: Noise Standard Deviations ---
noise_levels = [0.0, 0.1, 0.5, 2.0, 5.0]
quality_labels = ["Clean (No Noise)", "Slightly Noisy", "Visible Distortion", "Very Noisy (Masked)", "Almost Lost (Pure Noise)"]

# --- 3. Simulation & Plotting ---
plt.figure(figsize=(12, 10), facecolor='white')
plt.suptitle("Basic Communication System (Tx – AWGN Channel – Rx)", fontsize=15, fontweight='bold')

for i, (sigma, label) in enumerate(zip(noise_levels, quality_labels)):
    # Generate Additive White Gaussian Noise (AWGN)
    noise = np.random.normal(0, sigma, len(t))
    rx_signal = tx_signal + noise
    
    # Calculate Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR) in dB
    signal_power = np.mean(tx_signal**2)
    noise_power = np.mean(noise**2) if sigma > 0 else 1e-12
    snr_db = 10 * np.log10(signal_power / noise_power) if sigma > 0 else float('inf')
    
    plt.subplot(len(noise_levels), 1, i + 1)
    plt.plot(t, rx_signal, color='#2563eb' if sigma < 1.0 else '#dc2626', linewidth=1.2, label=f"Rx (σ={sigma})")
    if sigma > 0:
        plt.plot(t, tx_signal, color='#94a3b8', linestyle='--', linewidth=1.0, alpha=0.7, label="Original Tx")
    
    snr_text = f"SNR = {snr_db:.1f} dB" if sigma > 0 else "SNR = ∞ (Ideal)"
    plt.title(f"Noise Level σ = {sigma} — Quality: {label} ({snr_text})", fontsize=10, fontweight='bold', loc='left')
    plt.xlabel("Time (seconds)", fontsize=9)
    plt.ylabel("Amplitude (V)", fontsize=9)
    plt.grid(True, linestyle=':', alpha=0.6)
    plt.legend(loc='upper right', fontsize=8)

plt.tight_layout(rect=[0, 0.03, 1, 0.96])
plt.show()

print("=" * 60)
print("TX - CHANNEL - RX SIMULATION COMPLETED")
print("=" * 60)
for sigma, label in zip(noise_levels, quality_labels):
    print(f"Noise std dev σ = {sigma:<4} | Quality: {label}")
print("=" * 60)

vivaQuestions.q: What are the three fundamental blocks of any communication system?
vivaQuestions.a: Transmitter (Tx) which encodes and modulates the information, Channel which is the transmission medium, and Receiver (Rx) which detects and recovers the message.

vivaQuestions.q: What is AWGN?
vivaQuestions.a: AWGN stands for Additive White Gaussian Noise. It is 'Additive' because it adds linearly to the signal, 'White' because it has a flat power spectral density across all frequencies, and 'Gaussian' because its amplitude probability distribution follows a normal bell curve.

vivaQuestions.q: What happens to the received waveform when noise standard deviation increases to 5.0?
vivaQuestions.a: The noise power heavily overwhelms the signal power (resulting in a negative SNR in dB), completely masking the sinusoidal periodicity until the waveform appears purely random.

vivaQuestions.q: What is Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR)?
vivaQuestions.a: SNR is the ratio of signal power to noise power, typically expressed in decibels: SNR (dB) = 10 log10 (P_signal / P_noise).

conclusion: The simulation of a basic communication system (Tx-Channel-Rx) was successfully performed. In a wireless communication system, the transmission channel introduces white noise which directly degrades signal quality. As the noise standard deviation increases, signal distortion increases and amplitude fluctuates, causing the received waveform to transition from clean to completely lost.

name: Demonstration of Cellular Frequency Reuse Concept
problemStatement: Demonstrate and visualize the frequency reuse concept in a hexagonal cellular network layout for cluster size N=7, calculating the co-channel frequency reuse ratio Q = √(3N) and reuse distance D to optimize capacity while suppressing co-channel interference.
tasks: Define regular hexagonal geometry with normalized cell radius R = 1.0.
Select cluster size N = 7 (using N = i² + ij + j² with i=2, j=1).
Generate center coordinates for a 2D pointy-top hexagonal cell grid.
Assign frequency groups F1 through F7 across the grid using reuse formula: group = (m + 2n) mod N + 1.
Calculate theoretical frequency reuse ratio Q = √(3N) and reuse distance D = Q × R.
Plot the cellular layout with distinct cell shading and centered frequency group labels.
Compare performance across cluster sizes N = 3, 4, 7, and 9 in the observation table.

variants.description: Complete Python equivalent of the MATLAB script using matplotlib polygons with color-coded co-channel clusters and exact D/R ratio calculations.
variants.code:
"""
Demonstration of Frequency Reuse Concept in Cellular Systems
Subject: Modern Digital Mobile Communication
Language: Python 3 with Matplotlib & NumPy
"""
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.patches as patches

# --- 1. System Parameters ---
R = 1.0              # Normalized cell radius
N = 7                # Cluster size (cells per cluster)
Q = np.sqrt(3 * N)   # Frequency reuse ratio D/R = sqrt(3N)
D = Q * R            # Co-channel reuse distance

# Distinct harmonious color palette for co-channel clusters F1 to F7
cluster_colors = [
    '#fee2e2', '#fef3c7', '#dcfce7', '#e0e7ff',
    '#f3e8ff', '#fce7f3', '#ccfbf1'
]

# Hexagonal geometry (pointy-top orientation)
theta = np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi, 7) + np.pi / 6
hx = R * np.cos(theta)
hy = R * np.sin(theta)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 9), facecolor='white')
ax.set_aspect('equal')

count = 0
x_indices = range(-3, 4)
y_indices = range(-3, 4)

for m in x_indices:
    for n in y_indices:
        # Center coordinates for pointy-top hexagonal grid
        xc = 1.5 * R * m
        yc = np.sqrt(3) * R * (n + 0.5 * (m % 2))
        
        # Skip cells outside display boundary radius
        if np.sqrt(xc**2 + yc**2) > 5.5 * R:
            continue
            
        count += 1
        # Frequency group repeating assignment rule
        group = (m + 2 * n) % N + 1
        fill_color = cluster_colors[(group - 1) % len(cluster_colors)]
        
        # Draw hexagon polygon patch
        hex_patch = patches.Polygon(
            np.column_stack([xc + hx, yc + hy]),
            closed=True,
            facecolor=fill_color,
            edgecolor='#1e293b',
            linewidth=1.3,
            alpha=0.9
        )
        ax.add_patch(hex_patch)
        
        # Add bold frequency group label
        ax.text(
            xc, yc, f"F{group}",
            ha='center', va='center',
            fontsize=10, fontweight='bold',
            color='#0f172a'
        )

ax.set_xlim(-6.5 * R, 6.5 * R)
ax.set_ylim(-6.5 * R, 6.5 * R)
ax.grid(True, linestyle='--', alpha=0.4)
ax.set_title(
    f"Cellular Frequency Reuse Pattern (Cluster N = {N}, D/R = {Q:.2f})\n"
    f"Normalized Cell Radius R = {R:.1f}, Co-channel Reuse Distance D = {D:.2f}",
    fontsize=12, fontweight='bold', pad=15
)
ax.set_xlabel("Distance (normalized)", fontsize=10)
ax.set_ylabel("Distance (normalized)", fontsize=10)

print("=" * 50)
print("CELLULAR FREQUENCY REUSE DEMONSTRATION (PYTHON)")
print("=" * 50)
print(f"Cluster size (N)               : {N}")
print(f"Normalized cell radius (R)     : {R:.2f}")
print(f"Reuse ratio (Q = sqrt(3N))     : {Q:.4f}")
print(f"Reuse distance (D = Q * R)     : {D:.4f}")
print(f"Total displayed hex cells      : {count}")
print("=" * 50)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

observationTables.subtitle: Comparison of frequency reuse metrics across common hexagonal cluster sizes
rows: A smaller cluster size yields high frequency reuse and capacity, but co-channel cells are closer, resulting in greater co-channel interference.
Reuse distance increases compared with N=3, moderately reducing co-channel interference while maintaining reasonable capacity.
Provides an optimal balance between network spectral capacity and co-channel interference suppression; standard in cellular network planning.
Substantially larger reuse distance minimizes co-channel interference, but reduces channel allocation per cell and spectral efficiency.

vivaQuestions.q: What is frequency reuse in cellular communication?
vivaQuestions.a: Frequency reuse is the technique of utilizing the same radio frequency channels in different geographical cells that are sufficiently separated so that co-channel interference remains within acceptable thresholds.

vivaQuestions.q: What is a co-channel cell?
vivaQuestions.a: Cells in a cellular network that share the exact same set of operational frequency channels are known as co-channel cells.

vivaQuestions.q: What is the formula for cluster size N?
vivaQuestions.a: N = i² + i×j + j², where i and j are non-negative integers representing the number of hexagonal cell steps taken along axes to locate the nearest co-channel neighbor.

vivaQuestions.q: What is the co-channel reuse ratio Q?
vivaQuestions.a: Q = D / R = √(3N), where D is the distance between the centers of nearest co-channel cells and R is the cell radius. A larger Q means greater separation and less interference.

vivaQuestions.q: Why are regular hexagons chosen for cellular network geometry?
vivaQuestions.a: Hexagons tessellate (cover a 2D plane without overlaps or gaps), closely approximate the circular radiation footprint of omnidirectional antennas, and have the highest area-to-perimeter ratio among tessellating regular polygons.

conclusion: The frequency reuse concept was successfully demonstrated using MATLAB and Python. By partitioning a geographic service area into hexagonal cells and reusing identical frequency groups at safe separation distances (D/R = 4.58 for N=7), cellular networks achieve multiplied subscriber capacity over fixed, limited radio spectrum.

vivaQuestions.q: What does SSID stand for?
vivaQuestions.a: SSID stands for Service Set Identifier. It is the human-readable 32-character maximum name assigned to a Wi-Fi wireless local area network.

vivaQuestions.q: What is RSSI and why are its values negative?
vivaQuestions.a: RSSI stands for Received Signal Strength Indicator, measured in dBm (decibels relative to 1 milliwatt). Since received wireless signals are tiny fractions of a milliwatt (microwatts or picowatts), the log ratio 10 log10 (P_rx / 1mW) produces negative numbers. Values closer to 0 dBm represent stronger signals.

vivaQuestions.q: Which signal is stronger: -45 dBm or -75 dBm?
vivaQuestions.a: -45 dBm is substantially stronger. In fact, -45 dBm is 30 dB higher than -75 dBm, representing 1000 times more received signal power.

vivaQuestions.q: Why are channels 1, 6, and 11 standard in 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi?
vivaQuestions.a: Each standard 2.4 GHz 802.11 channel requires 20–22 MHz of spectral width, but channels are spaced only 5 MHz apart. Channels 1, 6, and 11 are spaced 25 MHz apart, meaning they are the only three completely non-overlapping channels that avoid adjacent-channel interference.

vivaQuestions.q: Does a high RSSI value always guarantee high internet download speed?
vivaQuestions.a: No. RSSI only measures raw signal power between the mobile device and the local Wi-Fi router. Internet speed also depends on backhaul ISP bandwidth, channel congestion, packet loss, and server response time.

conclusion: Nearby Wi-Fi networks were successfully scanned using a mobile Wi-Fi analyzer. The SSID, RSSI, channel, and frequency band parameters were recorded, and a channel map was constructed. The experiment clearly demonstrated that channel 6 was heavily congested with 4 co-channel networks, whereas 5 GHz channels (such as channel 157) offered superior signal strength (-61 dBm) with minimal interference due to wider channel allocation.

name: Measurement of Signal Strength vs. Distance for Wi-Fi Router
problemStatement: Measure and record the received signal strength (RSSI in dBm) of a Wi-Fi router at various distances (from 1m to 174m) to analyze signal attenuation, empirical indoor path-loss behavior RSSI(d) ≈ RSSI(d0) - 10n log10(d/d0), and environmental multipath fading.
tasks: Position the Wi-Fi router at a fixed location with constant orientation.
Connect an Android smartphone to the target Wi-Fi network.
Launch a mobile Wi-Fi analyzer tool to observe real-time RSSI readings.
Measure RSSI at incremental distances (~7m, ~24m, ~61m, ~87m, ~174m) maintaining consistent smartphone height.
Allow readings to stabilize and record RSSI (dBm) and signal quality rating.
Plot Distance (m) on the X-axis versus RSSI (dBm) on the Y-axis.
Analyze the logarithmic drop in signal power and explain deviations caused by walls, obstacles, and multipath reflections.

steps.title: Establish the Transmitter Baseline
steps.description: Place the Wi-Fi router at a fixed elevated location in the lab or corridor. Ensure its antennas remain vertically oriented throughout testing.

steps.title: Mark Measurement Distances
steps.description: Using a measuring tape or laser distance meter, mark inspection points at increasing distances: ~7m, ~24m, ~61m, ~87m, and ~174m from the router.

steps.title: Measure and Record Stable RSSI Values
steps.description: At each designated measurement point, hold the smartphone stationary at chest height for 5–10 seconds until RSSI stabilizes. Note the reading in dBm.

steps.title: Plot the Distance vs. Signal Strength Curve
steps.description: Plot Distance (m) on the horizontal X-axis and RSSI (dBm) on the vertical Y-axis. The resulting curve exhibits a characteristic logarithmic drop conforming to the log-distance path loss model: RSSI(d) ≈ RSSI(d0) - 10n log10(d/d0).

vivaQuestions.q: What happens to Wi-Fi signal strength as distance from the router increases?
vivaQuestions.a: Signal strength drops exponentially in linear units (inversely with the square of distance in free space, or higher powers in indoor environments), appearing as a linear downward slope on a logarithmic (dBm vs. log-distance) scale.

vivaQuestions.q: What is the log-distance path loss model?
vivaQuestions.a: It models indoor signal attenuation: PL(d) [dB] = PL(d0) + 10·n·log10(d/d0) + X_sigma, where d0 is a reference distance, n is the path loss exponent (typically 2 for free space, 3–5 for indoor obstructed environments), and X_sigma is shadowing noise.

vivaQuestions.q: Why doesn't RSSI always decrease smoothly with distance in indoor buildings?
vivaQuestions.a: Because of multipath propagation (reflections from walls, ceilings, and floors causing constructive and destructive interference), obstacle penetration losses (doors, concrete columns), and dynamic human movement.

vivaQuestions.q: What is the typical disconnection threshold for standard Wi-Fi devices?
vivaQuestions.a: Most mobile Wi-Fi client chips disassociate or drop packet communication when RSSI falls below approximately -85 dBm to -90 dBm.

conclusion: Wi-Fi signal strength was successfully measured at varying distances from 7m to 174m using a mobile Wi-Fi analyzer. The findings confirm that received signal strength decreases with distance, dropping from -57 dBm (Good) at 7m down to -85 dBm (Very Weak) at 174m. Minor non-linear fluctuations observed were attributable to indoor wall obstructions and multipath reflections.

vivaQuestions.q: What is Bluetooth and which standard governs it?
vivaQuestions.a: Bluetooth is a short-range wireless communication technology governed by the IEEE 802.15.1 standard and maintained by the Bluetooth Special Interest Group (SIG).

vivaQuestions.q: Which frequency band is used by Bluetooth?
vivaQuestions.a: Bluetooth operates in the 2.4 GHz ISM band (2.402 GHz to 2.480 GHz) divided into 79 channels (1 MHz each for Classic) or 40 channels (2 MHz each for Bluetooth Low Energy).

vivaQuestions.q: What modulation technique does Bluetooth use to resist interference?
vivaQuestions.a: Bluetooth uses Frequency Hopping Spread Spectrum (FHSS), hopping pseudo-randomly 1600 times per second across channels to avoid Wi-Fi and microwave interference.

vivaQuestions.q: What is Bluetooth pairing?
vivaQuestions.a: Pairing is the authentication process where two devices verify a shared secret (passkey or PIN) to create an encrypted, trusted relationship and store a shared Link Key for future automatic reconnection.

vivaQuestions.q: What are the typical power classes of Bluetooth?
vivaQuestions.a: Class 1: up to 100 mW (100 m range); Class 2: standard for smartphones, up to 2.5 mW (~10 m range); Class 3: up to 1 mW (~1 m range).

conclusion: Bluetooth communication between two mobile smartphones was successfully established through discovery and passkey verification. A test file was transferred with zero data loss. Range testing demonstrated that Bluetooth Class 2 devices maintain excellent performance up to ~3 meters (-57 to -69 dBm), but signal strength degrades to -80 dBm (Weak) at ~11 meters as distance and obstacle attenuation increase.

"""
Bluetooth Data Transfer Performance & Throughput Analysis
Subject: Modern Digital Mobile Communication
"""
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# --- Experimental Data from Lab Observation ---
file_types = ['Text', 'Image', 'Audio', 'Video', 'Large Video']
file_sizes_mb = np.array([1, 5, 10, 25, 50])        # in Megabytes (MB)
transfer_times_s = np.array([1.2, 3.5, 7.0, 18.0, 37.0]) # in seconds

# --- Calculations ---
# Transfer rate in Megabytes per second
rate_mbps = (file_sizes_mb / transfer_times_s) * 8  # Megabits per second (Mbps)
rate_mBps = file_sizes_mb / transfer_times_s        # Megabytes per second (MB/s)

print("=" * 65)
print(f"{'File Type':<15} | {'Size (MB)':<10} | {'Time (s)':<10} | {'Rate (Mbps)':<12} | {'Rate (MB/s)':<10}")
print("=" * 65)
for ftype, size, time, r_mbps, r_mBps in zip(file_types, file_sizes_mb, transfer_times_s, rate_mbps, rate_mBps):
    print(f"{ftype:<15} | {size:<10.1f} | {time:<10.2f} | {r_mbps:<12.2f} | {r_mBps:<10.2f}")
print("=" * 65)
print(f"Average Effective Bluetooth Throughput: {np.mean(rate_mbps):.2f} Mbps")

# --- Visualizing Performance ---
fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 5), facecolor='white')

# Subplot 1: File Size vs. Transfer Time
ax1.plot(file_sizes_mb, transfer_times_s, 'o-', color='#2563eb', linewidth=2, markersize=7)
ax1.set_title("File Size vs. Transfer Time", fontsize=12, fontweight='bold')
ax1.set_xlabel("File Size (MB)", fontsize=10)
ax1.set_ylabel("Transfer Time (seconds)", fontsize=10)
ax1.grid(True, linestyle='--', alpha=0.5)
for x, y, label in zip(file_sizes_mb, transfer_times_s, file_types):
    ax1.annotate(f"{label}\n({y}s)", (x, y), textcoords="offset points", xytext=(0, 8), ha='center', fontsize=8)

# Subplot 2: File Size vs. Transfer Rate (Mbps)
ax2.plot(file_sizes_mb, rate_mbps, 's-', color='#059669', linewidth=2, markersize=7)
ax2.set_title("Effective Transfer Rate (Throughput)", fontsize=12, fontweight='bold')
ax2.set_xlabel("File Size (MB)", fontsize=10)
ax2.set_ylabel("Transfer Rate (Mbps)", fontsize=10)
ax2.grid(True, linestyle='--', alpha=0.5)
ax2.axhline(np.mean(rate_mbps), color='#ea580c', linestyle=':', label=f"Mean: {np.mean(rate_mbps):.2f} Mbps")
ax2.legend(loc='lower right')

plt.suptitle("Bluetooth File Transfer Performance Analysis", fontsize=14, fontweight='bold')

"""

Subject: Modern Digital Mobile Communication
"""
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# --- Experimental Data ---
conditions = ['Clear LOS', 'Glass Partition', 'Wooden Door', 'Human Body', 'Concrete Wall']
avg_rssi = np.array([-48.0, -53.2, -58.4, -62.6, -71.8])  # in dBm
ref_rssi = avg_rssi[0]                                     # Reference LOS = -48.0 dBm
path_loss_db = -(avg_rssi - ref_rssi)                      # Additional path loss in dB

print("=" * 60)
print(f"{'Condition':<18} | {'Avg RSSI (dBm)':<15} | {'Additional Loss (dB)':<20}")
print("=" * 60)
for cond, rssi, loss in zip(conditions, avg_rssi, path_loss_db):
    print(f"{cond:<18} | {rssi:<15.1f} | {loss:<20.1f}")
print("=" * 60)

# --- Plotting Two-Panel Graph ---
fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 5), facecolor='white')

colors = ['#22c55e', '#3b82f6', '#f59e0b', '#ec4899', '#ef4444']

# Plot 1: Received RSSI (dBm)

# Plot 2: Relative Additional Path Loss (dB)
bars2 = ax2.bar(conditions, path_loss_db, color=colors, edgecolor='#1e293b', width=0.55)

vivaQuestions.q: What is indoor path loss?
vivaQuestions.a: Indoor path loss is the reduction in power density of an electromagnetic wave as it propagates through an indoor environment, caused by free space spreading, reflection, diffraction, and absorption by walls and furniture.

vivaQuestions.q: Why does a reinforced concrete wall cause much higher attenuation (~24 dB) than a wooden door (~10 dB)?
vivaQuestions.a: Because reinforced concrete has high dielectric permittivity and conductivity with dense rebar steel mesh, which causes intense reflection and skin-depth absorption of RF energy compared to low-density organic wood.

vivaQuestions.q: What is human body shadowing?
vivaQuestions.a: The human body is composed of approximately 60-70% water with dissolved electrolytes, which strongly absorbs 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz radio frequencies, causing 10 to 15 dB of shadowing loss when obstructing the line-of-sight.

conclusion: Path loss in an indoor environment was experimentally measured across various obstacle types at a fixed 5m distance. A clear Line-of-Sight yielded -48.0 dBm. Glass partitions introduced ~5.2 dB attenuation, wooden doors introduced ~10.4 dB, human body shadowing added ~14.6 dB, and a reinforced concrete wall introduced the greatest attenuation of ~23.8 dB, demonstrating the critical impact of building material composition on indoor wireless network coverage.

name: Effect of Noise and Interference on Wireless Communication
problemStatement: Simulate and analyze the Bit Error Rate (BER) performance of a Binary Phase Shift Keying (BPSK) digital wireless communication system over an Additive White Gaussian Noise (AWGN) channel and in the presence of continuous sinusoidal co-channel interference across an SNR range of 0 dB to 20 dB.
tasks: Generate a random binary information data sequence (N = 100,000 bits).
Perform Binary Phase Shift Keying (BPSK) modulation mapping {0 -> -1, 1 -> +1}.
Model Additive White Gaussian Noise (AWGN) with noise standard deviation sigma = sqrt(1 / (2 * SNR_linear)) across SNR from 0 dB to 20 dB in steps of 2 dB.
Model continuous sinusoidal co-channel interference: i(n) = A_int * sin(2 * pi * f_int * n) with f_int = 0.07 and amplitude 0.55.
Demodulate received signals using zero-threshold decision logic for both AWGN-only and AWGN + Interference channels.

variants.code:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

np.random.seed(1)

N = 100000
SNR_dB = np.arange(0, 22, 2)
A = 1

# Generate random binary data
data = np.random.randint(0, 2, N)

# BPSK modulation
tx = A * (2 * data - 1)

# Interference parameters
f_int = 0.07
int_amp = 0.55
n = np.arange(N)
interference = int_amp * np.sin(2 * np.pi * f_int * n)

ber_noise = []
ber_interference = []

for snr in SNR_dB:

    snr_linear = 10 ** (snr / 10)
    sigma = np.sqrt(1 / (2 * snr_linear))
    noise = sigma * np.random.randn(N)

    # Noise only
    rx1 = tx + noise
    detected1 = rx1 >= 0
    ber_noise.append(np.mean(detected1 != data))

    # Noise plus interference
    rx2 = tx + noise + interference
    detected2 = rx2 >= 0
    ber_interference.append(np.mean(detected2 != data))

# Display results
results = pd.DataFrame({
    'SNR_dB': SNR_dB,
    'BER_Noise_Only': ber_noise,
    'BER_Noise_Interference': ber_interference
})

print(results.to_string(index=False))

# Plot BER
plt.figure(figsize=(9, 5))

plt.semilogy(SNR_dB, ber_noise, '-o',
             linewidth=1.5, label='AWGN only')

plt.semilogy(SNR_dB, ber_interference, '-s',
             linewidth=1.5, label='AWGN + Interference')

plt.grid(True, which='both')
plt.xlabel('SNR (dB)')
plt.ylabel('Bit Error Rate (BER)')
plt.title('Effect of Noise and Interference on Wireless Communication')
plt.legend(loc='lower left')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

steps.description: Generate N = 100,000 uniformly distributed random binary bits {0, 1}. Modulate into antipodal BPSK baseband symbols using tx = A * (2*data - 1), mapping bit 0 to -1V and bit 1 to +1V.

steps.description: Create a deterministic sinusoidal interference vector interference = A_int * sin(2 * pi * f_int * n) where f_int = 0.07 and A_int = 0.55 across sample indices n = 0 to N-1.

steps.title: Iterate Over SNR & Inject AWGN
steps.description: For each SNR from 0 dB to 20 dB (step of 2 dB), compute linear SNR = 10^(SNR/10) and noise standard deviation sigma = sqrt(1 / (2 * SNR_linear)). Generate Gaussian noise vector noise = sigma * randn(1, N).

steps.title: Simulate Both Channels & Demodulate
steps.description: Construct received signals: rx1 = tx + noise (AWGN only) and rx2 = tx + noise + interference (AWGN + Interference). Apply zero-threshold detector detected = (rx >= 0).

steps.description: Calculate Bit Error Rate as the fraction of mismatched bits: ber = mean(detected ~= data). Format and display results in a structured table.

steps.title: Plot Comparative Semilogarithmic BER Curves
steps.description: Plot BER versus SNR using semilogy to observe the exponential decline in AWGN and the degradation / error floor created by co-channel interference.

vivaQuestions.q: What is the key difference between noise and interference in wireless communications?
vivaQuestions.a: Noise (such as AWGN) is an unpredictable, wideband random thermal process generated internally by electronic components and external blackbody radiation, modeled as Gaussian with zero mean. Interference is caused by unwanted man-made RF signals originating from other transmitters operating on the same frequency band (co-channel) or adjacent bands.

vivaQuestions.q: Why does the BER curve exhibit an error floor in the presence of interference?
vivaQuestions.a: Increasing signal SNR increases signal power relative to thermal noise, reducing thermal errors to zero. However, thermal SNR enhancement does not diminish the power of co-channel interference. When noise variance approaches zero, bit errors are entirely dictated by whether the interference amplitude exceeds the decision boundary, creating a persistent, flat BER floor.

vivaQuestions.q: What is the theoretical BER formula for BPSK over an AWGN channel?
vivaQuestions.a: For BPSK over an AWGN channel, the theoretical bit error probability is P_b = Q(sqrt(2 * E_b / N_0)) = 0.5 * erfc(sqrt(SNR_linear)). At 0 dB, theoretical BER is ~0.0786, closely matching our simulated result of 0.0774.

vivaQuestions.q: How can co-channel interference be mitigated in cellular networks?
vivaQuestions.a: Cellular networks mitigate co-channel interference through cellular frequency reuse planning (sufficient cluster size N), directional sector antennas (e.g. 120° or 60° tri-sector cells), dynamic power control, beamforming with Massive MIMO, and orthogonal multiple access schemes (OFDMA).

conclusion: The effects of Additive White Gaussian Noise (AWGN) and deterministic sinusoidal co-channel interference on digital wireless communication were successfully simulated using MATLAB and Python. In the AWGN-only channel, the BPSK Bit Error Rate decays rapidly from 0.0774 at 0 dB to 0.0000 at SNR >= 10 dB. In the presence of co-channel interference (amplitude 0.55), significant BER degradation is observed across all SNR values with an interference-dominated error floor persisting up to 14 dB SNR, demonstrating that interference, rather than thermal noise, is often the dominant capacity limiter in wireless cellular networks.

vivaQuestions.q: What is dBm and why is cellular signal strength expressed in negative numbers?
vivaQuestions.a: dBm is a logarithmic power unit referenced to 1 milliwatt (0 dBm = 1 mW = 0.001 W). Cellular received signal powers are very small, typically ranging between microwatts (10⁻⁶ W = -30 dBm) and picowatts (10⁻¹² W = -90 dBm). Because received power is fractions of a milliwatt, the log10 ratio is negative.

vivaQuestions.q: Why does a smartphone switch from 5G/4G to 3G or 2G in basements and elevators?
vivaQuestions.a: Higher carrier frequencies (such as 3.5 GHz for 5G or 1.8–2.3 GHz for 4G) suffer higher free-space path loss and severe penetration loss through thick concrete walls and metal enclosures. When signal power falls below the receiver sensitivity threshold for 4G/5G, the modem performs an Inter-Radio Access Technology (inter-RAT) handover to lower-frequency 2G/3G bands (e.g., 850/900 MHz) to maintain basic voice and SMS connectivity.

vivaQuestions.q: What is the physical cause of the extreme signal drop inside an elevator (-101 dBm)?
vivaQuestions.a: An elevator car acts as a metallic enclosure (Faraday cage), while the reinforced concrete elevator shaft creates intense shielding. The conducting metallic walls reflect and absorb electromagnetic waves, resulting in severe attenuation of up to 25–35 dB compared to open hallways.

vivaQuestions.q: What is the difference between RSSI, RSRP, and RSRQ in LTE/5G cellular systems?
vivaQuestions.a: RSSI (Received Signal Strength Indicator) measures total wideband received power including signal, interference, and thermal noise. RSRP (Reference Signal Received Power) measures the average received power of individual cell-specific reference resource elements (clean measure of signal strength). RSRQ (Reference Signal Received Quality) is the ratio of RSRP to RSSI (scaled by bandwidth), indicating channel interference and connection quality.

conclusion: Cellular signal strength was experimentally measured across 8 distinct indoor and outdoor campus environments using smartphone diagnostics. Received signal strength ranged from a peak of -61 dBm (5G, Open Area) down to -101 dBm (2G, Lift/Weak Area) with an overall average of -78.00 dBm. The experimental data confirms that Line-of-Sight conditions yield excellent 5G reception, whereas structural concrete walls, subterranean basements, and metallic elevator shafts induce significant attenuation (up to 40 dB loss), triggering automatic Inter-RAT cellular fallback to legacy 3G and 2G networks to avoid total connection drops.
